paragraphs.heading: The salt formers
paragraphs.text: The halogens are a group of six related elements: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, and the radioactive astatine and tennessine. Some authors leave tennessine out, because its chemistry is unknown. In modern IUPAC naming the group is called group 17. The word halogen means salt former, and when halogens react with metals they make many salts, such as calcium fluoride, table salt (sodium chloride), silver bromide and potassium iodide.

paragraphs.heading: An unusual group
paragraphs.text: At standard temperature and pressure, this is the only group of the table whose members span three main states of matter. Every halogen forms an acid when bonded to hydrogen. Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are nonmetals, while the chemistry of astatine and tennessine has not been settled. Chlorine, bromine and iodine often serve as disinfectants, and organobromides are the leading class of flame retardants. The pure elements, though, are dangerous and can be toxic.

paragraphs.heading: Capturing fluorine
paragraphs.text: Fluorspar, a mineral containing fluorine, was known as early as 1529. Early chemists could tell that fluorine compounds held an unknown element, but they could not get it out. In 1869 the English chemist George Gore sent an electric current through hydrofluoric acid and probably made fluorine, but he could not prove it then. In 1886 Henri Moissan in Paris succeeded, using electrolysis of potassium bifluoride dissolved in anhydrous hydrogen fluoride.

paragraphs.heading: Chlorine, bromine and iodine
paragraphs.text: Elemental chlorine was not made until 1774, when Carl Wilhelm Scheele warmed hydrochloric acid together with manganese dioxide, and in 1807 Humphry Davy found that it is a true element. In World War I chlorine served as a poison gas that burned tissue, especially the lungs. Antoine Jérôme Balard found bromine in the 1820s by passing chlorine gas through brine. In 1811 Bernard Courtois added sulfuric acid to his seaweed ash process and saw purple fumes condense into black crystals, which Joseph Gay-Lussac proved to be a new element, iodine.

paragraphs.heading: The heaviest members
paragraphs.text: Element 85 was claimed several times in the 1930s, under names such as alabamine and dakine, and every claim was wrong. It was finally produced in 1940 by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles, and it is now called astatine. Tennessine followed in 2010, when a team led by the nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian fired calcium-48 atoms at berkelium-249 atoms.

paragraphs.heading: Where the names come from
paragraphs.text: In 1826 the Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius proposed the word halogen for fluorine, chlorine and iodine. The English names of the halogens all end in -ine. Chlorine comes from the Greek for greenish-yellow, bromine from the Greek for stench, iodine from the Greek for violet, and astatine from the Greek for unstable. Fluorine comes from the Latin fluere, to flow, and tennessine is named after Tennessee, the US state where it was made.
